qa.name: Biceps Femoris
qa.origin: Long head: ischial tuberosity (common hamstring origin with semitendinosus). Short head: lateral lip of linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of femur
qa.insertion: Head of fibula; lateral condyle of tibia
qa.innervation: Long head: sciatic — tibial division (L5, S1, S2); Short head: sciatic — common fibular division (L5, S1, S2)
qa.function: Both heads: flex the knee and laterally rotate the leg. Long head only: extends and laterally rotates the hip
qa.opposing_muscle: Quadriceps (knee extension); iliopsoas (hip extension vs flexion)
qa.blood_supply: Perforating branches of profunda femoris; inferior gluteal artery (long head)
qa.clinical_note: Biceps Femoris has two heads with different nerve divisions — the long head from the tibial division and the short head from the common fibular (peroneal) division of the sciatic nerve. It is one of three hamstrings (with Semitendinosus and Semimembranosus). The hamstrings originate from the ischial tuberosity — except the short head of biceps femoris which originates from the femur, making it the only hamstring that does NOT cross the hip joint. Hamstring strains are the most common muscle injury in sport — typically at the proximal myotendinous junction.

qa.name: Biceps Femoris — Long Head
qa.origin: Ischial tuberosity (common hamstring tendon, shared with semitendinosus); sacrotuberous ligament
qa.insertion: Head of fibula; lateral condyle of tibia (with short head)
qa.innervation: Sciatic nerve — tibial division (L5, S1, S2); long head
qa.function: Extends and laterally rotates the hip; flexes and laterally rotates the knee
qa.blood_supply: Inferior gluteal artery; perforating branches of profunda femoris
qa.clinical_note: The long head is a true hamstring — crossing both the hip and knee joints. It shares the ischial tuberosity origin with semitendinosus (common tendon) and semimembranosus (separate tendon). Biceps Femoris is one muscle with two heads — the long head is innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve while the short head is innervated by the common fibular division. This dual innervation is a classic exam question. The long head is the most commonly injured hamstring muscle.

qa.name: Biceps Femoris — Short Head
qa.origin: Lateral lip of linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of femur
qa.insertion: Head of fibula; lateral condyle of tibia (with long head)
qa.innervation: Sciatic nerve — common fibular (peroneal) division (L5, S1, S2); short head
qa.function: Flexes and laterally rotates the knee only — does NOT act on the hip as it does not cross it
qa.clinical_note: The short head is the only hamstring muscle that does NOT originate from the ischial tuberosity and does NOT cross the hip joint — it originates from the femoral shaft. It is innervated by the common fibular (peroneal) division of the sciatic nerve, in contrast to the long head which is innervated by the tibial division. This makes Biceps Femoris unique among the hamstrings in having a split nerve supply. The two heads join distally to form a common tendon inserting on the fibular head — palpable on the lateral side of the popliteal fossa.

qa.name: Semitendinosus
qa.origin: Ischial tuberosity (common hamstring tendon, shared with long head of biceps femoris)
qa.insertion: Upper medial surface of tibia (pes anserinus — with sartorius and gracilis)
qa.innervation: Sciatic nerve — tibial division (L5, S1, S2); long cordlike tendon
qa.function: Extends and medially rotates the hip; flexes and medially rotates the knee
qa.opposing_muscle: Iliopsoas (hip flexion); quadriceps (knee extension); biceps femoris (lateral vs medial rotation)
qa.blood_supply: Perforating branches of profunda femoris; inferior gluteal artery
qa.clinical_note: Semitendinosus has a long slender tendon that occupies nearly half its length — hence the name. It inserts at the pes anserinus alongside sartorius and gracilis — mnemonic 'Say Grace before Tea'. Its tendon is commonly harvested as a graft for ACL reconstruction (along with gracilis) as it regenerates well and causes minimal donor site morbidity. It medially rotates the tibia, opposing biceps femoris which laterally rotates — important in rotational knee stability.

qa.name: Semimembranosus
qa.origin: Ischial tuberosity (separate flat membranous tendon, medial to semitendinosus origin)
qa.insertion: Posterior aspect of medial tibial condyle; also gives expansions to: posterior capsule of knee (oblique popliteal ligament), medial meniscus, and popliteus fascia
qa.innervation: Sciatic nerve — tibial division (L5, S1, S2); broad flat membranous origin
qa.function: Extends and medially rotates the hip; flexes and medially rotates the knee; tightens the posterior knee capsule
qa.blood_supply: Perforating branches of profunda femoris; inferior gluteal artery
qa.clinical_note: Semimembranosus has a broad flat membranous origin — hence the name — in contrast to the long cordlike tendon of semitendinosus. It has multiple insertions including the oblique popliteal ligament which reinforces the posterior knee capsule. A semimembranosus bursa can communicate with the knee joint and present as a popliteal (Baker's) cyst — a fluctuant swelling in the medial popliteal fossa, common in osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis. It lies deep to semitendinosus in the posterior thigh.
